client: I’ve been feeling really anxious about my presentation at the annual conference next week. Yesterday during practice, I completely forgot my lines, and it’s been stuck in my head ever since. I’m worried it’ll happen again during the actual presentation, and I’m not sure if talking about it here will really help me feel any better.
therapist: I hear the worry in your voice as you share this experience—it sounds like that moment of forgetting your lines really shook your confidence. Let's explore what thoughts are coming up when you imagine presenting, and we can look at ways to prepare that might help you feel more secure.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I keep replaying that moment in my head—it’s like I froze, and everyone was staring at me. I’m terrified it’ll happen again, and I’ll embarrass myself even more. I’ve thought about practicing more, but what if that doesn’t help? It feels like no matter what I do, I’ll just mess up again.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense as you describe this—it's clear how deeply this fear of freezing up again is affecting you. Let's examine the evidence: how often have you actually frozen in past presentations versus just this one recent time?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess I've only frozen that one time, but it felt so awful that now I'm convinced it'll happen every time. Even thinking about presenting again makes my chest tighten up - like my brain just goes blank all over again. 

But when you put it that way... I did give three other presentations last semester that went fine. It's just hard to remember those when the bad one sticks out so much.
therapist: Your voice sounds heightened as you describe the tightness in your chest—it’s understandable how vivid that one experience feels compared to the others. It might help to focus on what went well in those past presentations and explore what made them different from this recent one.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, moderate-paced speech

client: I get what you're saying about focusing on past successes, but this last presentation just felt so much worse than the others. Even thinking about those good presentations makes me anxious now because I'm scared I'll never be able to do that well again. The tightness in my chest comes back just remembering how I froze up last time.
therapist: Your voice sounds strained as you describe this—it's clear how strongly that one experience has overshadowed your previous successes. Let's look at what specifically felt different about that presentation compared to your others—sometimes naming those differences can help put things in perspective.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I guess what felt different was how quiet the room got afterward. In my other presentations, people would at least nod or ask a few questions, but this time there was just... nothing. It makes me wonder if I completely missed the mark or if they just hated what I had to say. 

Trying to analyze it now just makes me more anxious, like I'm reliving that awful silence. Is it really helpful to pick apart something that already feels so humiliating?
therapist: Your voice speeds up as you describe that silence—it sounds like that moment really left you feeling exposed and uncertain. Let’s shift focus for a moment: what’s one small step you could take to reclaim a sense of control over how you feel about presenting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I could try practicing my presentation more beforehand, but honestly, it’s hard to feel like that would help. Even when I prepare, I still feel like everyone’s judging me, and the silence just makes it worse. It’s like no matter what I do, I can’t shake that feeling of being exposed.
therapist: Your voice sounds flat and defeated as you say this—it’s clear how much that fear of judgment is weighing on you. Let’s explore what specifically makes you feel “exposed” when presenting—sometimes breaking down that feeling can help us find ways to make it more manageable.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, moderate-paced speech

client:
I don't know... it's like my throat closes up when I see all those eyes on me. I keep imagining people thinking "wow, she's terrible at this" or "why did they even put her in charge of presenting?" It's not just nervousness - it feels like physical pain sometimes. 

The worst part is I know my material cold when I'm alone, but the second I stand up there, my mind goes blank and I feel like everyone can see right through me. It's humiliating.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and strained as you describe this—it's clear how physically overwhelming this experience becomes for you when you're up there. Let's pause for a moment: when you notice your throat closing up, what’s one small thing you could do to help ground yourself in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I feel like when I’m up there, everything happens so fast that I don’t even have time to think about grounding myself. My throat closes up, and it’s like my brain just shuts down. I guess I could try to take a deep breath, but even that feels impossible in the moment—like I’m fighting to get air in.
therapist: Your voice sounds tight and breathless as you describe this—it makes sense that even thinking about breathing feels impossible when you're in that panicked state. Let's try something different: instead of waiting until you're up there, could you practice pausing and taking one slow breath during your preparation sessions too? That way, it might feel more automatic when the moment comes.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try that, but I don't know if it'll help when it really counts. During practice I'm already calm, so breathing slowly feels fake—like I'm just pretending. When I'm actually about to present, my mind goes totally blank and all the practiced stuff flies out the window.
therapist: Your voice sounds hesitant and a bit deflated as you share this—it makes sense that practicing when you're calm might feel disconnected from the intensity of the actual moment. What if we tried pairing those breaths with something that does trigger your nerves slightly during practice, to help bridge that gap?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I see what you're saying, but even the thought of intentionally triggering my nerves makes me feel panicky. I worry that if I purposely make myself anxious during practice, I won't be able to calm back down. It feels like playing with fire - like I might lose control completely.
therapist: Your voice sounds both hesitant and higher-pitched as you describe this—it’s understandable that the idea of triggering your nerves feels too risky right now. Let’s take a step back—what’s one small way you could practice staying present that feels safe and manageable to you?
